why_company: Voice is the interface I keep building toward. Kepler, my open-source Android app, turns EPUBs into narrated books with sentence-level read-along highlighting. Narration runs through a Media3 player, long chapters are generated in the background with WorkManager, and readers choose between offline system TTS and neural voices. Before that I built a voice-controlled desktop agent that streams speech both ways to the Gemini Live API over WebSockets, with noise reduction and adaptive silence detection. Both projects taught me that latency, sync and graceful failure decide whether voice feels magical or broken. ElevenLabs sets the quality bar for that whole category. A full-stack role there means working on the product layer that turns a great model into something people use every day, and that is the work I want to do.
impact_project: Kepler, an open-source (GPL-3.0) Android app for reading, listening to and remembering books, which I designed and built on my own in Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. The hard problem was keeping everything anchored to the text, because bookmarks, highlights, audio sync and flashcards all break when a book re-paginates. I solved it with a "Text Spine": deterministic sentence and paragraph IDs that every feature shares as one coordinate system. On top of it sit a Readium 3.4 reader with SQLite FTS5 search, a Media3 read-along player (0.5x to 3.5x, lock-screen controls, sleep timer), WorkManager background narration with time and cost estimates, and FSRS-6 spaced repetition. The AI features go through an "AI Fence" that clips every LLM prompt to the reader's current position, so summaries and recaps can never spoil unread chapters. API keys are encrypted with Android Keystore AES-256-GCM, and the app has no telemetry. It is split into app, core, engine and feature modules, and each module has its own unit tests.
success_measure: Each Kepler module has unit tests that run through Gradle, so a regression in the EPUB, TTS, playback, AI or spaced-repetition engines shows up before it reaches the app. The architecture also makes correctness something I can check rather than hope for. A highlight, bookmark or audio position is just a deterministic Text Spine ID, so I can change the typography, re-paginate, and confirm each one still lands on the same sentence. The AI Fence is enforced where the prompt is assembled, not by asking the model to behave, so verifying it means inspecting the assembled context and confirming that nothing past the reading position is in it.
product_usage: Not in a shipped project yet. Kepler's neural narration currently runs on Fish Audio, alongside offline system TTS. Its narration pipeline (background generation, per-sentence alignment for read-along, cost estimates before generating) is exactly where ElevenLabs' long-form, timestamped speech would plug in, and that is the integration I'd build first.
